title: Crosswords episode, perhaps?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and mechanics of crossword puzzles, starting with Josh's recent passion for the New York Times crossword. They cover Arthur Wynn's 1913 "word cross" in the New York World, the name change to "crossword," Margaret Petherbridge's early rules (symmetry, no unchecked squares, black-square limits set by the Amateur Crossword Puzzle League of America), Simon & Schuster's 1924 puzzle books, 1920s backlash, British cryptic crosswords, the New York Times adopting a puzzle in 1942 under Petherbridge, later editors Will Weng, Eugene Maleska and Will Shortz, and how puzzles are themed and constructed. They also give solving tips and crossword conventions (plurals, tense, quotes, brackets, heteronyms), discuss constructor submissions and diversity, the documentary Wordplay and the American Crossword Puzzle Tournament, and crosswords and brain health. The episode closes with a listener mail correcting an earlier claim that possums eat ticks.
topics: Amateur Crossword Puzzle League of America

entities.name: Amateur Crossword Puzzle League of America

segments.title: Opening banter and Josh's crossword passion
segments.summary: Josh describes taking up the New York Times crossword in 2022 and working up to all seven days; the hosts tease the history of the New York Times and its late adoption of crosswords.

segments.title: Arthur Wynn and the invention of the word cross
segments.summary: Arthur Wynn, a British immigrant who ran the Fun section of the New York World, published the 1913 diamond-shaped word cross. An illustrator's swapped title became 'crossword,' and Wynn did not patent it.

segments.title: Margaret Petherbridge and early crossword rules
segments.summary: Wynn's secretary Margaret Petherbridge codified crossword rules, including symmetry of black squares, separate across and down lists, and no unchecked squares. The hosts debate symmetry and the diagonal pattern.

segments.title: Simon and Schuster books and the Amateur Crossword Puzzle League
segments.summary: Simon and Schuster published crossword books in 1924 that sold well, and created the Amateur Crossword Puzzle League of America. Its rules limited black squares to one sixth of the grid and barred cut-off sections.
topics: Amateur Crossword Puzzle League of America

segments.title: Black squares debate and grid mechanics
segments.summary: The hosts argue about how black squares affect grid length and word length, with Chuck clarifying fifteen-by-fifteen grids and Josh noting constructors use few blanks and long words.

segments.title: 1920s crossword backlash and cryptic crosswords
segments.summary: Crosswords drew criticism in the 1920s, including a New York Times column calling them a sinful waste of time. The hosts then describe British cryptic crosswords and their wordplay, with an example clue for Chagall and another for eagle.

segments.title: New York Times crossword debut and later editors
segments.summary: In 1942 Margaret Petherbridge wrote to the New York Times arguing crosswords would distract during wartime, and she became its first editor for 27 years. Will Weng followed, then Eugene Maleska, whose opera-heavy clues alienated some solvers, and Will Shortz took over in 1993.

segments.title: Clue style, themes, and days of the week
segments.summary: The hosts discuss clever, solvable clues versus obscure trivia, Shortz's changes such as bylines, teen constructors and brand names, the progressive difficulty from Monday to Saturday, and themed puzzles.

segments.title: Solving tips, conventions, and puzzle construction
segments.summary: Tips include starting with known answers, using plurals and past-tense hints, learning abbreviations and partner clues, and using quote, bracket, question mark and heteronym conventions. The hosts also explain how Times puzzles are built by teams, and how submissions and acceptance rates work.

segments.title: Wordplay, brain health, and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts recommend the documentary Wordplay and the American Crossword Puzzle Tournament, discuss studies on crosswords and dementia, and close with a listener mail correcting the claim that possums eat ticks, citing a study finding no evidence of tick consumption in wild possums.
